Docker — Clean Training Notes

Consolidated from the supplied Docker text and DOCX notes. Class/date timestamps and repeated separators have been removed, and related topics have been reorganized into a clean teaching and revision structure.

1. Docker Fundamentals

Docker is described in the supplied notes as an open-source containerization platform used to create, deploy and run applications using containers.

What is a container?

A Docker container is a standardized unit that can be created to deploy a particular application or environment. The notes describe a container as a running instance of an image and as writable.

Why Docker?

  • Application agility
  • Developer productivity
  • Easy modeling
  • Operational efficiencies
  • Placement and affinity
  • Version control
Core concept: package the application and its dependencies into an image, then run that image as a container.

2. Containers vs Virtual Machines

Virtual MachinesContainers
Need more resources.Need fewer resources.
Process isolation is described at hardware level.Process isolation is described at OS level.
Need to pre-allocate memory.Memory is allocated automatically.
Separate OS for each VM.OS resources can be shared.
Take more time to create.Creation is much faster.
Booting time is more.Booting time is less.

The notes emphasize that VMs are more isolated but are heavier, while containers share the underlying kernel and are lightweight.

3. Docker Architecture

The supplied notes describe four main parts: Docker Client, Docker Daemon, Docker Host and Docker Registry, with the client and daemon communicating through the Docker REST API.

ComponentRole
Docker ClientInterface used to interact with Docker and send commands to the daemon.
Docker DaemonBackground process that manages Docker objects such as images, containers, networks and volumes.
Docker HostMachine where Docker is installed and where the daemon, images and containers run.
Docker RegistryStores Docker images and supports pulling and pushing images.
REST APIInterface through which clients communicate with the Docker daemon.
The source architecture diagram also shows Docker objects such as images, containers, networks and volumes being managed through the client/REST API/daemon layers.

4. Docker Images, Containers and Registry

Docker Image

A Docker image is a package containing the application code, libraries, tools, dependencies and other files required to run an application. The notes describe image layers as read-only.

Docker Container

A container is the running state/instance of a Docker image. Containers package the application together with dependencies and configuration.

Image Registry

A registry is an area where Docker images are stored. It can be public or private. The notes identify Docker Hub as a public registry and also discuss Amazon ECR and JFrog.

Repository vs Registry

RepositoryRegistry
Collection of related container images used to manage, pull and push images.Collection of repositories used to store and distribute container images.

5. Essential Docker Commands

Images

docker search <image_name>
docker pull <image_name>
docker images
docker image ls
docker rmi <image_name_or_id>

Containers

docker ps
docker ps -a
docker rm <container_name_or_id>
docker run -it <image_name>
docker run -it --name <container_name> <image_name>
docker run -itd <image_name>
docker stop <container_name_or_id>
docker start <container_name_or_id>
docker start -i <container_name_or_id>

Interact with a container

docker exec <container_name_or_id> <command>

6. Container Interaction: exec vs attach

docker execdocker attach
Runs a new command/process inside a running container.Attaches the terminal to the container's main process (PID 1).
Useful when you want to run a command without entering the container.Connects directly to the core process of the container.

Exit without stopping the container

The notes describe using an escape sequence such as Ctrl+P followed by Ctrl+Q to detach while leaving the container running.

Custom detach keys

docker run -it --detach-keys ctrl-s <image_name>

7. Port Mapping and Container Networking Basics

Port publishing maps a host port to a container port.

docker run -it -p 8080:8080 <image_name>

# Multiple ports
docker run -p <host_port1>:<container_port1>            -p <host_port2>:<container_port2> <image_name>
Source terminology: the first port is described as the EC2/host port and the second as the container port.

8. Dockerfile and Build Context

A Dockerfile is a text document containing instructions used to create a custom Docker image. The default filename is Dockerfile.

Build commands

docker build .
docker build -f <Dockerfile_name> <path>
docker build -t <image_name>:<tag> .
docker build --tag="updatedubuntu" .

Build context

The context is the folder containing the dependencies/files available to the Docker build. The source notes commonly use . to represent the current directory.

.dockerignore

The .dockerignore file lists files and directories that should be excluded from the build context. The notes associate this with reducing image size and speeding up the build.

9. Dockerfile Instructions

InstructionPurpose from the supplied notes
FROMSpecifies the base/parent image. It can appear multiple times for multi-stage builds.
LABELProvides metadata.
ENVSets environment variables in the image/container environment.
RUNRuns commands during image build and creates an image layer.
COPYCopies files/directories from the build context into the image.
ADDCopies files/directories and, as described in the notes, can handle URLs and local tar archives.
CMDProvides the default command/arguments for a container. The notes state only the last CMD takes effect.
ENTRYPOINTDefines the execution point/command; runtime parameters are passed as arguments.
WORKDIRSets the working directory for subsequent Dockerfile instructions.
ARGDefines a build-time variable.
USERSwitches the user used inside the container.
SHELLOverrides the default shell used by shell-form instructions.
EXPOSEDocuments/exposes a container port; the notes specifically state it does not publish a host port.
VOLUMECreates a directory mount point for persistent data.

10. RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT

RUN

RUN executes commands while building the image. The source notes point out that each RUN creates an intermediate image layer and show chaining related package installations.

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y git && apt-get install -y wget

CMD

CMD supplies a default command when a container starts. The notes state that a runtime command can override CMD and that only the last CMD takes effect.

CMD /bin/bash
CMD ls
CMD ["echo", "hello"]

ENTRYPOINT

ENTRYPOINT defines the default execution point. Runtime parameters are treated as arguments to the configured entrypoint. The notes also show overriding it with --entrypoint.

ENTRYPOINT ["echo", "hello"]
docker run -it --entrypoint="<command>" <image_name>
Interview focus: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT
CMD provides default command/arguments that can be replaced by runtime command arguments; ENTRYPOINT is intended to remain the main executable while runtime arguments are appended to it.

11. COPY, ADD, ENV and ARG

COPY

COPY <source_path> <destination_path>
COPY --chown=<user>:<group> <source_path> <destination_path>

ADD

The notes describe ADD as supporting local files/directories, URLs and tar archives.

ADD <source_path> <destination_path>
ADD <URL> <destination_path>
ADD <tar_file> <destination_path>

ENV

ENV KEY=value
ENV KEY1=value1 KEY2=value2

docker run -it --env KEY=value <image_name>
docker run --env-file <path_to_env_file> <image_name>

ARG

ARG is used for values passed at build time.

docker build --build-arg user=bhavya --tag="arg" .

12. WORKDIR, USER, SHELL and EXPOSE

WORKDIR

Sets the working directory for subsequent instructions. The notes state that Docker creates it if necessary.

USER

Changes the user used inside the container. The source notes highlight the security concern of running applications as root.

SHELL

Overrides the default shell used for shell-form commands. The notes identify /bin/sh -c as the Linux default and cmd /S /C for Windows.

EXPOSE

Documents the port used by the container. The source explicitly distinguishes EXPOSE from publishing a host port.

13. COPY Files To/From Containers

The source notes provide docker cp for copying files between the host and a container.

# Host → container
docker cp <src-path> <container>:<destination_path>

# Container → host
docker cp <container>:<source-path> <local-destination_path>

14. Multi-Stage Docker Builds

Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM statements in one Dockerfile. Each FROM starts a new build stage, and selected artifacts can be copied from one stage into another.

Why use multi-stage builds?

  • Keep final images smaller.
  • Remove build tools and unnecessary dependencies from the final image.
  • Reduce the amount of content carried into the runtime image.

Source example: Java/Maven/Tomcat

FROM alpine AS git
RUN apk update && apk add git
WORKDIR /usr/java
RUN git clone https://github.com/adhig93/java_repo1
RUN git clone https://github.com/adhig93/tomcat-config

FROM maven:amazoncorretto AS maven
COPY --from=git /usr/java/java_repo1/src /usr/app/src
COPY --from=git /usr/java/java_repo1/pom.xml /usr/app/
RUN mvn -f /usr/app/pom.xml clean install

FROM tomcat
RUN cp -r webapps.dist/* webapps/
COPY --from=maven /usr/app/target/*.war /usr/local/tomcat/webapps/
COPY --from=git /usr/java/tomcat-config/context.xml /usr/local/tomcat/webapps/host-manager/META-INF/context.xml
COPY --from=git /usr/java/tomcat-config/context.xml /usr/local/tomcat/webapps/manager/META-INF/context.xml
COPY --from=git /usr/java/tomcat-config/tomcat-users.xml /usr/local/tomcat/conf
docker build -t tomcatmulti .
docker run -itd -p 8080:8080 tomcatmulti

15. Docker Volumes and Persistence

Container data can be lost when a container is removed. The notes use Docker volumes and bind mounts to persist data or share it between containers.

Docker-managed volume

docker volume create <volume_name>
docker volume ls
docker volume rm <volume_name_or_id>

docker run -it -v <volume_name>:<container_path> <image_name>

Bind mount

docker run -it -v <host_machine_path>:<container_path> <image_name>

Anonymous volume

The source notes describe an anonymous volume as one that is created automatically when running a container.

Volume advantages over bind mounts

  • Easier to back up or migrate.
  • Can be managed through Docker CLI/API.
  • Can be shared safely among multiple containers.
  • Work with Linux and Windows containers according to the source notes.

16. Docker Resource Limits

Memory

docker run -it --memory="1g" alpine
docker run -it --memory="1g" --memory-reservation="750m" alpine

The notes distinguish a hard memory limit from --memory-reservation and discuss OOM behavior.

CPU

docker run -it --cpus="1" alpine

Monitoring resource usage

docker stats
docker system df

Swap

The source notes describe --memory-swap as allowing additional memory requirements to use swap when RAM is exhausted.

17. Docker Networks

Docker networking allows containers to communicate with other containers and the Docker host and provides network isolation.

DriverSource notes
BridgeDefault/private internal network. Containers receive internal IPs and can communicate over the bridge.
HostRemoves network isolation and uses the host networking directly.
NoneContainer is not attached to a network; the notes describe complete network isolation.
OverlayPrivate network spanning nodes participating in a Swarm cluster.

Bridge commands

docker network ls
docker network create --driver bridge <network_name>
docker inspect <network_name>
docker run -it --network=<network_name> <image_name>
docker network connect <network_name> <container_name_or_id>
docker network disconnect <network_name> <container_name_or_id>

18. Bridge, Host and None Network — When to Use

Bridge

The notes describe the default bridge network as docker0. Containers on a bridge network have their own IP identity and host port mapping is used when external access is required.

Host

The host driver removes the network isolation between the host and container. The source notes associate this with higher performance but fewer isolation boundaries.

None

The none driver provides complete network isolation. The notes give batch jobs as one use case.

19. Docker Compose

Docker Compose is used to run multiple containers as a single service. The notes use a microservices/e-commerce example where web, database and other services run in separate containers but can interact.

Compose file

The source notes identify docker-compose.yml as the default filename and YAML as the configuration format.

version: "3.9"
services:
  frontend:
    build: .
    volumes:
      - "/home/ubuntu/test:/test"

  backend:
    image: jenkins/jenkins
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

Commands from the notes

docker-compose up
docker-compose up -f <filename>
docker-compose up -d
docker-compose down

20. Docker Swarm

Docker Swarm is described in the notes as a native Docker orchestration tool for managing containers across multiple hosts.

  • Uses overlay networks for inter-host communication.
  • Supports service discovery using DNS.
  • Allows a cluster of hosts to be managed as a resource pool.
docker swarm init --advertise-addr <manager_IP>

Compose vs Swarm

Docker ComposeDocker Swarm
Multiple containers as a service on a single host.Multiple containers/services across multiple hosts.
Uses a YAML file to define services.Provides cluster/orchestration capabilities.

21. Docker Prune and Dangling Images

Prune commands

docker system prune
docker image prune
docker container prune
docker volume prune
docker network prune

Dangling images

Dangling images are untagged images without a repository/tag association. The notes explain that repeated image builds can leave older intermediate images consuming disk space.

docker images -f dangling=true
docker image prune -a

22. Image Push: Docker Hub and Amazon ECR

Docker Hub

  1. Create a Docker Hub account.
  2. Run docker login.
  3. Build/tag the image with the repository name.
  4. Push the image.
docker login
docker build -t <username>/<repository>:<tag> .
docker push <username>/<repository>:<tag>

Amazon ECR

The notes describe creating an ECR repository, tagging the image with the ECR URI, authenticating with AWS CLI and pushing the image.

aws ecr get-login-password --region <AWS_region> | docker login   --username AWS   --password-stdin <ECR_URL>

docker tag <existing_image> <ECR_URL>:<tag>
docker push <ECR_URL>:<tag>
Credential hygiene: the supplied source contained access-key/secret-key/password-like values. Those values are intentionally not reproduced in the clean notes.

23. Docker Commit, Save and Load

Docker commit

Creates an image from an existing container.

docker commit <container_name_or_id> <image_name>

Export image to archive

docker save -o <exported_name>.tar <image_name>

Import an image archive

docker load -i <exported_image_name>.tar
The source notes use docker commit as the snapshot approach for a container and discuss save/load as an alternative for moving images.

24. Container Lifecycle and Restart Policies

Lifecycle

The notes list the lifecycle states/actions as: create, run, pause, unpause, start, stop, restart, kill and destroy.

Restart policies

PolicySource description
no/offContainer is not restarted automatically.
on-failureRestarts after a failure condition.
unless-stoppedRestarts unless it was explicitly stopped by the user.
alwaysRestarts regardless of failure/stopping conditions as described in the notes.
docker run -dit --restart=<restart-policy> <container_name>

25. Hypervisors and Containerization Concepts

Hypervisor

A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, creates and runs virtual machines and shares host resources among guest VMs.

Type 1 / Bare MetalType 2 / Hosted
Runs directly on computing hardware.Runs within the host operating system.

Linux cgroups and namespaces

The source notes describe cgroups as a kernel mechanism for limiting/measuring resources such as CPU and memory for groups of processes. Namespaces provide isolation such as visibility, network interfaces, user IDs and mounts.

StatelessStateful

28. Docker with Jenkins / Shared Library

The source notes include a Jenkins Shared Library example for Docker integration. The shared library is intended to avoid repeating similar Jenkinsfile code across multiple microservices.

The supplied example uses Groovy and stores reusable logic under a shared-library structure, with Docker build, push and deployment stages.

def call(String registryCred = 'a', String registryin = 'a',
         String docTag = 'a', String contName = 'a',
         String grepo = 'a', String gbranch = 'a',
         String gitcred = 'a') {
    pipeline {
        environment {
            registryCredential = "${registryCred}"
            registry = "$registryin"
            dockerTag = "${docTag}_$BUILD_NUMBER"
            containerName = "${contName}"
            gitRepo = "${grepo}"
            gitBranch = "${gbranch}"
            gitCredId = "${gitcred}"
        }

        agent { label 'docker' }

        stages {
            stage("POLL SCM") {
                steps {
                    checkout(...)
                }
            }

            stage('BUILD IMAGE') {
                steps {
                    script {
                        dockerImage = docker.build("$registry:$dockerTag")
                    }
                }
            }

            stage('PUSH HUB') {
                steps {
                    script {
                        docker.withRegistry('', "$registryCredential") {
                            dockerImage.push()
                        }
                    }
                }
            }

            stage('DEPLOY IMAGE') {
                steps {
                    script {
                        docker.withRegistry('', registryCredential) {
                            dockerImage.run(...)
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
The source notes explain that shared libraries help multiple microservices reuse mostly identical pipeline code while allowing project-specific inputs.

29. Docker + Maven + Tomcat Multi-Stage Workflow

The supplied training notes combine Git checkout, Maven build and Tomcat runtime into a multi-stage image. The overall flow is:

Git source
   ↓
Build stage
   ↓
Maven clean install
   ↓
WAR artifact
   ↓
Tomcat runtime image

The source also contains a single-image Tomcat exercise where the container is entered, required webapps content is prepared, and then docker commit is used to create a new image.

30. Interview Questions and Quick Revision

What command lists only stopped containers?
docker ps -a -f status=exited
How do you display only container IDs?
docker ps -q
How do you display IDs of stopped containers?
docker ps -aq -f status=exited
How do you check Docker client/server versions?
docker version
What does docker info show?
Detailed Docker host information such as containers/images and their state plus host/kernel/resource information.
What is the difference between EXPOSE and publish?
EXPOSE documents the container port; -p/--publish maps a host port to a container port.
How do you exit a container without stopping it?
Use the configured detach escape sequence, such as Ctrl+P followed by Ctrl+Q in the source notes.
Can a paused container be removed?
The source answer says the container must first be stopped.
What is the lightest image according to the notes?
The source notes identify Alpine.
What are common containerization tools mentioned?
The source notes mention Docker and OpenShift, and later list Packer and Nomad in an interview-question context.
Why use .dockerignore?
To exclude unnecessary files/directories from the build context, reducing build context size and helping build performance.

31. Practical Assignments

  1. Create a Dockerfile using Ubuntu as the base image and clone a Git repository.
  2. Explain and demonstrate docker exec vs docker attach.
  3. Map multiple host/container ports.
  4. Practice COPY and ADD.
  5. Practice WORKDIR, USER, SHELL and EXPOSE.
  6. Push an image to Docker Hub.
  7. Push an image to Amazon ECR.
  8. Create a multi-stage Java/Maven/Tomcat build.
  9. Practice Docker volumes and bind mounts.
  10. Study Linux cgroups and namespaces.
